newsitem.title: INDONESIA: OPINION-Indonesian paper maker Tjiwi Kimia expands.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Indonesian paper maker Tjiwi Kimia expands.

text.p: By Lita Syukur, Pulp and Paper Analyst
Paribas Asia Equity, Indonesia

JAKARTA, July 16 - PT Pabrik Kertas Tjiwi Kimia (Tjiwi Kimia), the paper manufacturing arm of Indonesia's second largest conglomerate, the Sinar Mas group, is entering another phase of expansion with installed capacity to more than double in 1998.
Coupled with the predicted improvement in paper prices and a focus on more value-added products, the outlook for sales and profits is a bright one.
Tjiwi plans to use proceeds of $250 million from the recent rights issue to finance a new paper machine (PM11) with a capacity of 370,000 tonnes.

The company expects the machine to begin commercial production by the second quarter of 1998, thereby more than doubling total capacity installed and boosting production volumes by 30 percent to 773,100 tonnes from 557,000 tonnes in 1997.

Due to a lower machine utilisation rate of 91 percent from 93 percent previously, we have adjusted down our paper sales volume expectations for 1997, but as PM11 comes on stream in 1998, volumes shoot up.
We conservatively assume only a 50 percent utilisation rate in 1998 compared to the company's prediction of at least 75 percent, leaving room for future upgrades.
MORE MATT PAPER IMPROVES SALES MIX

With the company planning to produce more matt paper to keep up with the Off Machine Coater which started operations in December 1996, and continually looking for higher prices and margins than for base paper, we assume that matt paper sales will increase from nine percent of total 1996 sales to 19 percent in 1997 and 23 percent in 1998.

In line with the greater capacity plus management's decision to focus more on value-added products, e.g. stationery products such as loose leaf paper, spiral notebooks, notepads and exercise books, we have also increased our stationery sales volume assumption from 96,708 tonnes to 100,269 tonnes in 1997.
In the first quarter of 1997, Tjiwi was able to produce 38,000 tonnes (up 81 percent yoy) and sell 23,000 tonnes (up 53 percent yoy).
Moving into 1998, Tjiwi can easily achieve full production capacity of 150,000 tonnes, thus underpinning sales volume growth of 31.6 percent.

With the additional capacity of 370,000 tonnes from PM11, the company can choose to either increase volume in matt paper (which we are currently assuming) or to increase volume in stationery or a combination of the two.
However, this would mean adding a new stationery converting machine in 1998. The company is looking at possibilities to do this, but there are no details available yet.
PAPER PRICES FOLLOW PULP PRICES...UP

With a successful increase in pulp prices implemented throughout the region from May 1 and a second price hike announced on July 1, we expect to see paper prices move up as well, passing through the increase in raw material cost to the consumer, albeit with a few weeks' lag.

Accordingly we have increased our price assumptions for cast-coated paper, art/matt paper and NCR paper by about six percent and base paper (woodfree) by about two percent in 1997, thus bringing total average paper selling price of $1,027 per tonne compared to $986 per tonne previously.
We have looked at a number of scenarios which show that it is justifiable to produce more value added products, e.g. matt paper.
If we assume that the company produces and sells more base paper (60 percent) and reduces matt paper by 10 percent, we forecast that bottom line in 1998 will be nine percent lower.

Conversely, if we assume than more matt paper (30 percent) and less base paper (40 percent) is sold, then net profit in 1998 would be 15 percent higher, justifying the expansion into more value added products.
BUT NOT SO TO EXPORT PRICES
Traditionally, Tjiwi has exported more than 50 percent of its total paper production, with Asian countries the main destination.
The share of exports of matt paper has increased from 20 percent in 1994 to 58 percent in 1996, with export prices slightly lower (five percent) than the domestic price in the latter year.

This compares to a more usual higher export price in previous years and for other paper products. If export prices continue to stay below domestic prices and/or drop further, there is a good chance that less matt paper will be exported.

However, Tjiwi is not really very sensitive to the lower export price. If we assume that in 1998 and 1999, Tjiwi exports 70 percent of production compared to the current assumption of 58 percent, then net profit would only be about 1.0 percent and 1.1 percent lower respectively.
The commitment of management of Tjiwi Kimia to expand into value-added products and improve selling prices is the key to future success.

Based on our recently upgraded forecasts which factor in better than expected first quarter results and the recent rights issue, Tjiwi offers impressive turnover and EPS growth of 47 percent in 1998, diluted to a still healthy 30 percent if warrant conversion is taken into account.
With this growth and a current PER of 11.6x 1997 earnings and 7.9x 1998, the stock is inexpensive. We recommend BUY.
(NOTE-The views expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters).
